canonical_record.label: Bose et al. gravitational entanglement test proposal
canonical_record.summary: Bose and collaborators proposed a test in which gravitationally induced phase evolution between two micron-size test masses in adjacent matter-wave interferometers could produce detectable entanglement, with the masses separated sufficiently to keep Casimir-Polder forces at bay.

sources.title: A Spin Entanglement Witness for Quantum Gravity

statement: Bose and collaborators proposed a test in which gravitationally induced phase evolution between two micron-size test masses in adjacent matter-wave interferometers could produce detectable entanglement, with the masses separated sufficiently to keep Casimir-Polder forces at bay.

scope.population: Two micron-size test masses in adjacent matter-wave interferometers, as described in the proposal by Bose and collaborators.
scope.time: The paper was submitted on 19 July 2017. This date identifies the proposal's publication history and does not establish the date of an experimental observation or its current frontier standing.
scope.assumptions: The proposed arrangement relies on gravitationally induced phase evolution between the test masses, with sufficient separation to keep Casimir-Polder forces at bay. Detectable entanglement is a prediction within the proposed setup, not a reported measurement.
scope.uncertainty: The retained source presents a theoretical proposal and predicted test outcome. It does not report that the experiment was performed, that the entanglement was observed, or that gravity's quantum nature was experimentally established. Status reported attributes the proposal to its authors; era undated leaves atlas chronology unresolved; frontier false makes no claim about current research leadership.
scope.quantifiers: The prediction is limited to the two-mass interferometric arrangement described in the paper. No universal assertion about all gravitational interactions or all proposed gravity tests is made.

support.quote: Here, we introduce an idea for such a test based on the principle that two objects cannot be entangled without a quantum mediator.

We show that despite the weakness of gravity, the phase evolution induced by the gravitational interaction of two micron size test masses in adjacent matter-wave interferometers can detectably entangle them even when they are placed far apart enough to keep Casimir-Polder forces at bay.
